listing_view.reasoning: Book-building demand ran hot: subscription went from under 1x on day two to 30.8x by mid-morning on day three, which typically signals strong HNI/QIB interest at the close and supports a listing pop. The issue is small (~₹631 million), which amplifies price moves either way. The caveat is that this demand arrived in a single late surge, and I have no anchor, GMP or basis-for-price data to confirm the band is fair.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue and PAT are both shrinking over two years (latest revenue down 24%), ROCE has halved to 10.6% and ROE to 7.6% — the last is below what the same capital could earn in riskless instruments. Worse, reported EBITDA of ₹2,162 million came with NEGATIVE operating cash flow of ₹1,970 million in the latest year, and receivable days have quadrupled to 137, so the profits are increasingly accounting entries, not cash. Unless receivables are collected and margins hold, this is a deteriorating earnings stream.

governance.reasoning: The company, a SEBI-registered investment adviser, has a live SEBI show cause notice in the Enforcement Adjudication pipeline (SCN dated 2025) and separately paid a ₹4 lakh SEBI penalty, and there is a disclosure hook for disciplinary action against promoters [litigation, page 608], [litigation, page 610]. That is not disqualifying but it is regulator attention on the very regulated activity the company conducts, disclosed at materiality-threshold length, not explained in the extracts I was given.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Latest-year operating cash flow is -₹1,970 million against ₹1,320 million PAT, and receivable days ballooned from 35 to 137 — the earnings quality is collapsing and a funding squeeze becomes possible if customers keep stretching.

A SEBI show cause notice to a company whose core licence is a SEBI registered Investment Adviser registration, plus a prior penalty, could threaten the right to operate the regulated business or impose conditions that hit revenue.
Revenue fell 24% in the latest year and ROCE/ROE are on a declining path to 10.6%/7.6%, so an IPO multiple on peak-year earnings would embed a recovery the statements do not show.
No basis-for-price chapter or peer valuation was provided, so there is no way to test whether ₹159–167 is a fair price; the asking price must be assumed to be the seller's optimum.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Primarily receivables: customers now take 137 days to pay versus 35 days two years ago, which is the clearest explanation for the ₹8,166 million swing in operating cash flow across three years. Inventory cannot be ruled in or out — the extracts contain no inventory line item — but the customer-payment data on its own is sufficient to explain most of the cash absorption.

answers.question: who are the customers, and is any of it disputed?
answers.answer: Not answerable from what I was given. The business chapter extracts show revenue totals and a 'Trading Activity and Order Book Representation' heading but name no customers, disclose no concentration, and mention no disputed receivables — yet receivables stretching to 137 days combined with a SEBI enforcement track makes customer quality the single most important unanswered question.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the 137-day receivables are from a small number of high-grade institutional counterparties collected shortly after year-end, and satisfactory resolution of the SEBI show cause notice, would turn the long-term view around. Conversely, disclosure that the offer is predominantly an offer for sale, or that the receivables are ageing further, would push a decent listing into a 'take the pop and leave' trade.
